steps.title: Key Fact
steps.body: Cinematography encompasses all visual choices made with the camera to create meaning and emotion in film.

steps.title: Key Fact
steps.body: Camera shots are defined by distance: extreme long shot establishes setting, long shot shows full body, medium shot frames waist-up, close-up fills the frame with face or object, extreme close-up isolates a tiny detail.

steps.title: Key Fact
steps.body: Camera angles communicate power and status: low angles make subjects appear powerful and dominant, high angles make them seem vulnerable or small, eye-level angles feel neutral and objective.

steps.title: Key Fact
steps.body: Dutch or canted angles create unease, disorientation and psychological instability, commonly used in horror and thriller genres.

steps.title: Check your answers
steps.body: A low-angle shot positions the camera below eye level looking up at the subject, making them appear powerful, dominant or threatening. steps.title: Exam tips
steps.body: Always link cinematography choices to meaning — never just identify a technique, explain its effect on the audience. Use precise terminology: say 'low-angle shot' not 'shot from below', and 'shallow focus' not 'blurred background'. Compare cinematography across scenes or films to show how different choices create different meanings. When writing about lighting, consider whether it is motivated by an in-film source or unmotivated and purely atmospheric. Think about how cinematography works with other film language elements — a close-up is more powerful when combined with diegetic silence.
